Pocket-sized worlds, drawn in liquid crystal.

Before the Game Boy, Nintendo's Game & Watch turned every shirt pocket into a tiny arcade. NintendoGame.Watch is a fresh tribute to that decade-long experiment in lateral thinking — every series, every model, every quirk, gathered in one place.

Why it matters

A masterclass in doing more with less.

Lateral Thinking
Calculator-watch logic

Gunpei Yokoi looked at a bored businessman fidgeting with a calculator and saw an entire product category. Game & Watch was built from cheap watch parts and LCD segments — and changed handheld gaming forever.

A Decade of Risks
Ten distinct hardware ideas

Two screens, curved mirrors, transparent LCDs, head-to-head play, colour overlays — Nintendo treated every series like a small experiment. Some sold by the million. Some are now museum pieces.

Living Pixels
Quietly disappearing

The LCD fluid in many units is failing forty years on. NintendoGame.Watch keeps each model documented, photographed, and findable — so the shapes and stories survive even when the screens fade.

D-Pad Origins
A cross that conquered gaming

The Multi Screen Donkey Kong of 1982 introduced the plus-shaped directional pad — invented because the clamshell had no room for four discrete buttons. Every controller since, from the NES to the Switch, is a refinement of that one decision.

Hardware Lineage

Ten series, one idea, eleven years.

Each series tried something Nintendo had never built before — a new form factor, a new display trick, or a new way to play. From a single juggler in 1980 to Mario juggling under a moonlit stage in 1991. Tap any entry to drop into its catalogue.

About

The Game & Watch, in our words

NintendoGame.Watch is a love letter to a small, strange family of handhelds Nintendo built between 1980 and 1991 — a decade in which a games company that mostly made playing cards and toys quietly invented modern portable gaming.

The first unit, Ball, slipped out of Japan on the 9th of April 1980. It cost a few thousand yen, ran on watch batteries, and let you keep a juggler from dropping two stiff little balls. It sold a million copies. By the time the line ended in 1991, Nintendo had shipped fifty-nine different models across ten distinct hardware series, and posted somewhere north of forty-three million units sold worldwide.

"Lateral thinking with withered technology." — Gunpei Yokoi's design philosophy. Take old, cheap, well-understood parts; find a brand-new use for them.

The man behind the magic

Gunpei Yokoi joined Nintendo in 1965 as a maintenance engineer. He went on to lead the R&D1 group responsible for the Game & Watch, the Game Boy, and Metroid. The story goes that he watched a bored salaryman on a Shinkansen passing time by tapping the buttons of a calculator, and wondered if you could put a tiny game in the same pocket-sized shell. The Game & Watch is what came out the other side.

Yokoi left Nintendo in 1996 and died in a road accident the following year. His fingerprints are still on every handheld Nintendo ships.

Acknowledgements

This site is built on the work of a lot of people, and it owes them thanks.

Nintendo and the late Gunpei Yokoi's R&D1 team made the machines in the first place. Everything here is a tribute to them; the Game & Watch name, games and characters remain their property.

The MAME project is the backbone of the hardware research. The Sharp SM5A / SM500 / SM510 / SM511 / SM512 CPU cores emulated here were ported and cross-checked against MAME's own src/devices/cpu/sm510 device source (BSD-3-Clause, copyright hap), and each device's on-screen geometry follows MAME's own layout. Facts throughout the Hardware tabs are drawn from that code and from Sharp's original SM-series data books. The game ROMs themselves were recovered from real silicon by hardware preservationists — above all Sean Riddle, whose chip decapping, die photography and ROM dumps (seanriddle.com) are where the Sharp ROMs these emulators run came from, and whose die-level pinouts independently confirmed much of the Hardware-tab detail and corrected our supply-rail labelling.

The Game & Watch artwork — the vector LCD layouts, unit art and printed backgrounds that make every device recognisable — is the work of the MAME artwork community, above all hydef, who authored and refined the SVG layouts across the whole line, and DarthMarino, who contributed the colour backgrounds and Crystal Screen button art. It was released and discussed on the MAMEWorld artwork thread; where a piece ships with a README naming its artist, that credit holds. Our thanks to everyone who contributed there.

Special thanks to nintendogameandwatch.com for the device photography — the reference shots of the physical units throughout this collection. It is the most thorough Game & Watch photo archive on the web, and this site would look far poorer without it.

The two colour 35th-anniversary units — the Mario and Zelda TFT handhelds — run a hand-built ARM digital twin that leans on the Game & Watch retro-go homebrew community and on ST's published notes for the STM32 on-the-fly decryption engine.

If your work is represented here and you would like it credited differently, do reach out and it will be put right.

Settings
Version 1.2.0
No passwords. No accounts. Just a vault code.

This site doesn't use logins or sign-ups. Your collection — notes, prices, photos, receipts — is saved against a single random vault code (a UUID) that lives in this browser's storage. Anyone who knows the code can read and edit the vault; nobody else can. Save it in a password manager so you can paste it into another browser or device later. If you lose the code, the data is unrecoverable — there's no email + password reset, because there's no email or password.

Choose how the site looks. Dark is the default — it's like viewing the units in a dim room. Light brightens everything, and gives the see-through Crystal Screen units their proper light look. Your choice is remembered on this device.

The highlight colour used across the site — a unit marked as collected, the glow when you hover a tile, the drawer's section headers, buttons and links. The default is the classic green.

The playable emulators need each device's ROM, segment artwork and — for the Mario and Zelda colour units — firmware, none of which ships with the site. Open a single .zip of your own dumps, segment SVGs and colour-unit flash here, and the site identifies everything by its content and brings the emulators to life. It's all kept on this device — nothing is uploaded.

This code is the only key to your data. Save it in a password manager. Anyone with it can read and edit your vault.

Generates a brand-new vault code and replaces the current one. Your data, files, and email stay where they are — only the code that unlocks them changes. Save the new code immediately — there's no recovery if you lose it.

Stored against this vault only so a future "send me my code" recovery can reach you. Not used for login. You can leave this blank.

If you saved a recovery email against a vault, enter that address and we'll mail the code to it. Pasting the received code into Switch to a different vault (Access Code tab) gives you back in.

Backup downloads one JSON file with every device row, every photo, every receipt, and your recovery email — your entire vault, embedded. Restore wipes the current vault then loads everything back from a backup file. Keep the file somewhere safe — it's everything.

Anyone with your share URL can view your collection — collected ticks, public notes, grades, photos — without ever seeing your vault code, private notes, prices, or receipts.

Reset URL generates a fresh share URL — existing recipients lose access, anyone you give the new one to gains it. Disable sharing turns the whole feature off; all share URLs go dead until you re-enable.

Sharing is currently OFF. No share URL works.

Permanently deletes this vault — every device record, every uploaded photo and receipt, the recovery email, and the vault itself. There is no undo. If you might want this data back, take a Backup first.

Boot your own firmware
